title: Dhu Husan, Where Fartana Lived, Has Faded, and So Have al-Fawari'
intro: Al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani addresses al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir after word of the king's anger reaches him far from court. Faint traces of Fartana's camp give way to the sleeplessness of a snakebitten man, then to an oath sworn by the camels bearing pilgrims. Ibn Rashiq counts the odes in 'ayn and ba as two of al-Nabigha's apologies to the king. In Muhammad Abu al-Fadl Ibrahim's edition this ode has thirty-three verses, which Osama al-Nahari recites in order. The separate twelve-verse apology opens with words heard partway through this one, “Word reached me, may you be spared a curse.”

translation: Dhu Husan, where Fartana lived, has faded, and so have al-Fawari',
the two flanks of Arik and the channels that carry the floods.
1.sharh: He follows Fartana's former dwelling places across a named landscape. The eye moves from the sides of a height into the channels that drain it, where water can erase what people leave behind.

translation: And where the watercourses meet, the traces have been changed
by summers that passed after us, and springs.
2.sharh: At the meeting of the channels he can name what happened in their absence. More than one summer and more than one spring have acted on the marks of occupation.

translation: I searched out signs of her and recognised them
after six years, and this is the seventh.
3.sharh: Recognition takes work. He counts six whole years apart and the one now under way, setting the length of his memory against the faintness of its evidence.

translation: Ashes like eye kohl, just discernible,
and a trench like the broken, sunken base of a trough.
4.sharh: A dark pinch of ash marks the old fire. The earthen barrier once dug around the tent is as low and chipped as the stump of a watering trough.

translation: Where the burying winds dragged their skirts across it
lies a mat, it seems, patterned by women's hands,
5.sharh: Wind erases the human traces but makes patterns of its own. They are close and regular enough to look like the work of women weaving a mat.

translation: on a leather spread with new straps,
which a merchant carries through the perfume market.
6.sharh: The imagined mat gains a backing and a setting. A merchant shows it on fresh-strapped leather among dealers in fine goods, as if the patterns in the dust were valuable merchandise.

translation: I checked a tear and turned it back
onto my breast, some streaming, some still welling.
7.sharh: Trying to master the tears divides them into two kinds. Some glisten in his eyes while others are already running down onto his chest.

translation: At the very time I reproached grey age for youthful longing
and said, “Have I still not come to my senses, with grey hair a curb?”
8.sharh: He talks to himself as someone old enough to know better. Grey hair ought to rein in his youthful yearning, just as a graver anxiety is about to displace it.

translation: But a consuming worry had come between me and all that,
at the heart's covering, where searching fingers feel for it.
9.sharh: Anxiety lodges so deep in his chest that he imagines the probing fingers of someone trying to locate the hurt. What follows gives the pain its name.

translation: Abu Qabus's threat, out of all proportion,
reached me with Rakis and al-Dawaji' between us.
10.sharh: Abu Qabus is the king. The poet has given him no grounds for so great a threat, and the valleys between them have done nothing to keep its news away.

translation: I spent the night as if a slender snake had sprung at me,
a speckled one with deadly venom in its fangs.
11.sharh: The threat has the bodily effect of a venomous bite. In the old explanation a lean snake can be an old one whose venom has grown particularly potent.

translation: Through the longest night her bitten man is kept awake,
women's jewellery clattering on his hands.
12.sharh: The “safe one” is the traditional hopeful name for a snakebite victim. An old custom described by the commentators put women's ornaments on him, their clatter helping keep him awake.

translation: The charmers warn each other how evil her venom is.
One moment she releases him, the next she takes him back.
13.sharh: Even those who treat bites warn one another about this snake. The ebb and return of the venom's pain give the poet's fear a rhythm through the night.

translation: Word reached me, may you be spared a curse, that you blamed me,
and that is the news that stops the ears.
14.sharh: The traditional royal greeting interrupts a frightening message. This line shares its opening with another apology, but here the news is so terrible that the very organs of hearing close up.

translation: The report that you said, “I shall get at him”,
and such words from someone like you strike terror.
15.sharh: He finally lets the king's reported words be heard. Their force lies in who uttered them. A king needs only promise to lay hands on a man.

translation: By my life, and my life is no small thing to me,
the Aqari' have spoken falsely about me.
16.sharh: He puts his own life behind his denial and insists it is a costly stake. The accusers, left unnamed while he described his fear, come into view.

translation: The Aqari' of Awf, I mean no others,
monkey faces looking for someone to trade insults with.
17.sharh: He limits the charge to a particular branch of Awf. The caricature then turns their accusations into a readiness to pick a quarrel with anyone.

translation: A man came to you nursing hatred for me,
with another enemy like him to back him up.
18.sharh: Two voices in agreement might sound like corroboration at court. The poet supplies the missing connection between them. Both men want to injure him.

translation: He came with a lie of loosely woven cloth
and never brought the truth, bright and clear.
19.sharh: A loose weave shows daylight through the cloth. He invites the king to examine the allegation closely enough to see how little holds it together.

translation: He came with words I would never utter,
even with iron fetters locked on my forearms.
20.sharh: The denial extends to a case where he would have every reason to give in. Even iron binding his forearms could not force those words out of him.

translation: I swore to leave no doubt in your mind.
Would a man of faith sin of his own free will?
21.sharh: An oath places the truthfulness of the speaker at risk before a power above the king. The appeal depends on the idea that a man who acknowledges his duty would shrink from perjury.

translation: By the camels travelling together from Lasaf and Thabra,
bound for Ilal, pressing on together,
22.sharh: The sentence reaches back to “I swore”. Its witnesses are pilgrimage camels streaming from two named places towards the hill at Arafat.

translation: swift birds racing the wind, their eyes sunk deep,
worn-out mounts left like deposits along the road,
23.sharh: Speed has its cost. The camels that keep up seem like birds, but their eyes are hollow and other mounts have had to be left in the road's keeping.

translation: bearing dishevelled men intent on their pilgrimage,
the camels bowed like the tips of bows.
24.sharh: The rough-haired figures are pilgrims. The ones bending are their mounts, whose exhausted necks recall the curved ends of bows.

translation: You have laid another man's sin on me and let him go,
like the mangy camel grazing while another is branded.
25.sharh: He pictures responsibility landing on the wrong back. In the old comparison the animal with the disease grazes undisturbed while a sound one takes the branding iron.

translation: If the man who bears me spite is still believed against me,
and my oath of innocence does me no good,
26.sharh: The conditional sentence begins to close off his ways out. His enemy's word carries weight with the king while his own sworn word carries none.

translation: and nothing I say is trusted,
and you will inevitably carry out your purpose,
27.sharh: He has run through every argument he can make. Once the king is resolved and no statement wins his trust, the listener still has to wait one line for the result.

translation: then you are like the night that overtakes me,
though I thought there was room to get far from you.
28.sharh: Night does not need to pursue a traveller in order to reach him. The comparison makes the very extent of open country, his supposed escape route, part of the king's power.

translation: Crooked hooks on strong ropes,
drawn towards you by hands that haul,
29.sharh: Imagine him down a well. The hooks and the hands winding in their ropes make the reach of royal power into something he can feel pulling on him.

translation: Do you threaten a servant who kept your trust
and spare a wrongdoer who walks with a limp?
30.sharh: One servant has kept faith, while the man allowed to go free is guilty. Al-Nabigha makes his guilt as visible as a limp in his walk.

translation: You are a spring whose bounty brings people back to life,
and a keen sword lent to Death.
31.sharh: His gifts revive the needy as rain revives the land. The same king serves Death as a borrowed sword when the time comes for a life to end.

translation: God wills only justice and good faith from him.
Wrong wins no approval, and a good deed is never lost.
32.sharh: He bases his hope on a justice that recognises good service. The diwan's commentary also takes the pronouns as referring directly to God, whose justice the king is asked to honour.

translation: May you drink whenever you wish, with no stint,
from a curved cup with musk clinging around its rim.
33.sharh: The closing blessing gives the king a cup filled without stint and scented at the edges. The apologetic voice returns from sleepless terror to the ease of a royal gathering.

1.1.2-3.head: ذو حُسى
1.1.2-3.meaning: Dhu Husan, a place in the territory of Banu Murra.

1.1.5.meaning: Fartana, the woman whose former dwelling places he recognises.

1.1.6.head: الفَوارِع
1.1.6.meaning: Al-Fawari', uplands named among the abandoned sites.

1.2.2.head: أَريك
1.2.2.meaning: Arik, a height or locality whose two sides overlook watercourses.

1.2.3-4.head: التِّلاعُ الدَّوافِع
1.2.3-4.meaning: Channels that carry runoff down into the valleys.

2.1.2.head: الأَشراج
2.1.2.meaning: Water channels that run down towards a valley.

2.2.1.head: مَصايِف
2.2.1.meaning: Summers, or the winds that come with them.

3.1.1.head: تَوَهَّمَ
3.1.1.meaning: Scrutinised faint traces until they could be made out.

3.1.2.head: آيات
3.1.2.meaning: Recognisable marks of the old dwelling.

4.1.4.head: لَأي
4.1.4.meaning: Only with difficulty, after looking closely.

4.2.1.head: نُؤي
4.2.1.meaning: An earthen bank or trench protecting a tent against runoff.

4.2.2.head: جِذم
4.2.2.meaning: The stump or base left when the rest has fallen away.

4.2.4.head: أَثلَم
4.2.4.meaning: Chipped or breached along the rim.

5.1.2.head: مَجَرّ
5.1.2.meaning: The track left by something dragged along.

5.1.3.head: الرّامِسات
5.1.3.meaning: Winds that cover landmarks in dust.

5.2.3.head: نَمَّقَ
5.2.3.meaning: Patterned it with careful, decorative workmanship.

6.1.3.head: مِبناة
6.1.3.meaning: A leather spread on which wares can be displayed.

6.2.4.head: اللَّطيمَة
6.2.4.meaning: A market for cloth and perfume in Abu Amr's explanation. Abu Ubayda understands it as the caravan that carries perfume and other fine wares.

7.2.4.head: مُستَهِلّ
7.2.4.meaning: Tears that have broken out and are streaming.

8.1.6.meaning: The longings and impulses of youth.

8.2.5.head: وازِع
8.2.5.meaning: A curb or restraint on one's impulses.

9.2.2.head: الشِّغاف
9.2.2.meaning: The membrane around the heart, here the seat of anxiety.

10.1.2-3.head: أَبو قابوس
10.1.2-3.meaning: Abu Qabus, the byname of al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, king at al-Hira.

10.1.6.head: كُنه
10.1.6.meaning: The true nature or proper measure of a thing.

10.2.3.head: راكِس
10.2.3.meaning: Rakis, a valley evoked to mark the distance from the court.

10.2.4.head: الضَّواجِع
10.2.4.meaning: Al-Dawaji', places or bends in a watercourse, named alongside Rakis.

11.2.2.head: الرُّقش
11.2.2.meaning: Snakes with contrasting spots or markings.

12.1.3-4.head: لَيلُ التَّمام
12.1.3-4.meaning: “The full night”, the long midwinter night or a night prolonged by suffering.

12.1.5.head: سَليم
12.1.5.meaning: A snakebite victim, called “safe” in hope of recovery.

12.2.5.head: قَعاقِع
12.2.5.meaning: Clatters made by pieces of jewellery knocking together.

13.1.2.head: الرّاقون
13.1.2.meaning: Healers who recite charms over a snakebite.

13.2.1.head: طَلَّقَ
13.2.1.meaning: Lets him go for a time, as the effects of the bite abate.

14.1.2-3.head: أَبَيتَ اللَّعن
14.1.2-3.meaning: “May you refuse what earns a curse”, a traditional royal greeting.

14.2.3.head: اِستَكَّ
14.2.3.meaning: Close up or grow deaf to a sound.

15.1.6.head: نالَ
15.1.6.meaning: I shall get at him, a threat of punishment.

16.2.5.head: الأَقارِع
16.2.5.meaning: Al-Aqari', the branch of Tamim descended from Quray' ibn Awf whom he accuses.

17.1.2.head: عَوف
17.1.2.meaning: Awf, an ancestor identifying the particular branch he attacks.

17.2.5.head: جادَعَ
17.2.5.meaning: Trade abuse, from a verb associated with cutting off the nose.

18.2.6.head: شافِع
18.2.6.meaning: A backer who adds his testimony to another's.

19.1.3-4.head: هَلهَلُ النَّسج
19.1.3-4.meaning: “Loosely woven”, said of a report as flimsy as thin cloth.

19.2.6.head: ناصِع
19.2.6.meaning: Clear and unmistakable, originally pure white.

20.2.2.head: كَبَلَ
20.2.2.meaning: Were fastened tight, as with iron fetters.

21.2.4.head: إِمَّة
21.2.4.meaning: A religious commitment or rule of life.

22.1.1.head: مُصطَحِبات
22.1.1.meaning: Camels travelling in company, invoked in the oath.

22.1.3.head: لَصاف
22.1.3.meaning: Lasaf, a place in Tamim territory.

22.1.4.head: ثَبرَة
22.1.4.meaning: Thabra, named alongside Lasaf on the pilgrims' route.

22.2.2.head: إِلال
22.2.2.meaning: Ilal, a hill at Arafat on the pilgrimage route.

23.1.1.head: سَمام
23.1.1.meaning: Swift-flying birds, to which the camels are likened.

24.1.2.head: شُعث
24.1.2.meaning: Men rough-haired and dusty from travel, here the pilgrims.

24.2.4.head: خَواضِع
24.2.4.meaning: Holding their necks low after a long journey.

25.2.6.head: راتِع
25.2.6.meaning: Grazing at ease in good pasture.

27.2.4.head: مَحالَة
27.2.4.meaning: In the phrase la mahala, inevitably or without escape.

28.2.4.meaning: A place to which one can withdraw far away.

29.1.1.head: خَطاطيف
29.1.1.meaning: Hooks used to draw things up from a well.

29.1.2.head: حُجن
29.1.2.meaning: Curved or hooked at the tip.

30.2.5.head: ظالِع
30.2.5.meaning: Limping, a figure for a guilty man. Ibrahim prints ضالع, crooked or unjust, and also records ظالع, the form used here.

31.2.3.head: المَنِيَّة
31.2.3.meaning: Death, imagined borrowing a sword to take the lives due to it.

33.1.6.head: مُصَرَّد
33.1.6.meaning: One given less drink than would satisfy him.

33.2.1.head: زَوراء
33.2.1.meaning: Zawra', a curved or oblong drinking vessel, also explained as a royal residence in al-Hira.

33.2.5.head: كانِع
33.2.5.meaning: Close against the surface, clinging to the rim.
